analysis.one_liner: Lets college athletes earn money from their fame, join together to bargain, and license their group image.
analysis.headline: The College Athlete Economic Freedom Act never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee with zero cosponsors until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write into federal law the right of college athletes to be paid for the commercial use of their name, image, and likeness, and it would strip the NCAA and universities of the power to cap those payments or punish athletes for hiring agents. It would let athletes form a group representative — a players' association — to negotiate contracts and group licensing deals, and it would require schools and conferences to get a license, and disclose what they earn, whenever they use a group of athletes' images in media deals. It would also require donor-funded NIL collectives to register with the FTC and report, by gender, race, and sport, who actually gets the money, and it would give athletes the right to sue schools that violate these rules, with violations treated as antitrust violations.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes, especially those in the big-revenue sports whose images are used in televised games and advertising. Today an athlete can sign an individual endorsement deal, but schools and conferences still control the group uses — media rights agreements built on athletes' likenesses — and the NCAA has fought efforts to let athletes bargain collectively or be treated as employees. This bill would let athletes organize to negotiate those deals and would make it illegal for schools to collude to hold down what athletes are paid.

how_it_helps.text: Bars colleges and athletic associations from enforcing any rule that prevents college athletes, individually or as a group, from marketing their names, images, and likenesses, and bars schools from coordinating to cap what athletes are paid [S2].
Guarantees athletes the right to form a collective representative — a players' association or agents — to negotiate contracts and group licensing agreements, without losing eligibility [S2].

Requires schools and conferences to obtain a license from a group of athletes before using the group's image in any promotion, including media rights agreements, and to disclose how much revenue they receive from that use [S2].

Requires donor-funded NIL collectives to register with the FTC and report the number and dollar value of deals they facilitate, broken down by gender, race, and sport, and bars them from discriminating in who they pay [S2].
Makes violating these rights enforceable by the FTC, by an athlete's own lawsuit with attorney's fees, and as a per se Sherman Act violation [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The NCAA, college athletic departments, and conference media partners, who currently profit from athletes' images in televised games and promotions without group licenses. The bill would force group licensing payments, expose pay-coordination to antitrust suits, and apply FTC oversight to NIL collectives. Schools warn that sharing more revenue with athletes could squeeze budgets for non-revenue sports.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state laws governing athlete name, image, and likeness contracts, wiping out rules some states have already adopted, though states could keep certifying athlete agents [S2].

Treating a violation as a per se Sherman Act violation, with a private right of action and attorney's fees, could flood schools and conferences with litigation and destabilize how college sports finances are organized [S2].

If schools and conferences must pay athletes for group licensing, money could shift away from Olympic and non-revenue sports that depend on football and basketball revenue, which is the core objection schools raise to athlete compensation mandates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directly addresses a real imbalance: athletes whose images drive billions in media rights revenue have no right to bargain over those uses, while schools and conferences do. The costs fall on the institutions and broadcasters that currently keep that revenue, not on taxpayers. The genuine risks are litigation-heavy enforcement and possible funding pressure on non-revenue sports, and preemption of state NIL laws is a real trade-off. On balance, the bill's benefits to a group of unpaid performers in a money-making enterprise outweigh its costs, though its sweeping antitrust enforcement mechanism was an obvious point of resistance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the bill on July 26, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1][S4].
No cosponsors signed on from either party [S3].
No further action of any kind was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The NCAA and college athletic departments are better off: athletes may still sign individual endorsement deals, but the current system stands — no collective bargaining rights, no group licensing requirement for media rights deals, and no federal cap on what schools can coordinate to restrict. Athletes who wanted to organize collectively gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no senator joined him.

for.name: National College Players Association
for.what_they_did: Publicly supported athlete compensation and collective-bargaining rights legislation championed by Senator Murphy.

against.name: Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; it sat without a hearing or vote from referral until the Congress ended.

against.name: NCAA
against.what_they_did: Lobbied Congress for narrow federal NIL legislation with an antitrust exemption and against proposals treating athletes as employees with collective-bargaining rights.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic sponsor drew zero cosponsors from either party and no votes were ever taken, so the bill never became a partisan fight.

industries.note: The bill would strip their power to cap athlete pay, punish agent use, and control group uses of athletes' images, and would expose pay coordination to antitrust suits. They currently retain that revenue and control.
Schools would need group licenses, and disclosed revenue sharing, for media rights built on athletes' images. They argue this would divert money from non-revenue sports.

The bill legitimizes collectives as the channel for booster money while forcing FTC registration and reporting on who receives deals by gender, race, and sport. Their spending would remain concentrated in a few athletes without the bill's anti-discrimination mandate.
The bill bars schools from restricting athletes' access to agents and representatives, expanding their market. Their interest runs with athletes' right to representation.
